speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: So, Deborah, thank you very much and thank you for addressing this so very, very important issue for Northwest Indiana. At the backbone of Northwest Indiana, as I always mentioned is our steel industry and the United Steel Workers. It's also our building trades. It's also our construction trades. It's the iron workers it's electricians. It's many unions. It's the teachers unions. It's the postal workers. It's across the board. Unionization is something that is very important to working men and women across the first congressional district. So my background is first and foremost, my grandfather was a steel worker. He was in local 1010. He worked there for 55 years, came over from Czechoslovakia. My father, who was born and raised in the Chicago and became an Indiana State Senator, had a very high ranking and has a very high voting record for the unions and the AFL-CIO, and has consistently been a champion for working men and women. My predecessor, Congressman Viscowski, has set the bar at a very high level of being a champion and advocate for working men and women. and union labor throughout Northwest Indiana. There wasn't a union hall that you would walk into that you didn't hear people yelling Pete when he would walk in. And that was a sign of respect for him because he was one of them. And so we work every single day as a staff and as a member of Congress to make sure that we're protecting men and women who are in labor unions. In my past electoral experience, I was a township trustee that when there would be work stoppages or there would be strikes, we were on the at the picket lines, we were in the union halls making sure that you would have a safety net for those individuals who would run out of resources while that was going on or who were out of a job because of the global market or dumping from foreign countries. And so near and dear to my heart is making sure that we protect unions every single day. So this pro act, is something that we passed in the 117th Congress. It did pass last year. And so now it is on the Senate side waiting for a ratification or for it to be brought up as far as legislation. And I'm sure towards the end of the conversation, you may ask, well, what can we do to see to make sure that this passes and it's to contact the United States senators via email or phone call letting them know that you support this. And so the PRO Act is really something that is vital because it gives unions the right to collectively bargain. It gives them for a fair election. It also allows workers to stand together to form a union and to have the ability to use their collective voices for fair wages. Also what we always have to consider is safe work environments, trade unions and all unions put an emphasis on safety and making sure not only are things built on time on schedule but safely and that everyone who goes to a job returns home from that job. And so union labor also, something that I believe is near and dear to my heart. So I'm a freshman member of Congress, I get sworn in on January 3rd, I take an oath On January 6th, we have events happen the insurrection or the riots at the capitol. I only bring that up because consistently what I have been saying, and I mean this wholeheartedly, is that what I am here to do is to close that gap, chip away at that divide. So what was very, very clear was that there's a divide in our nation. And very often workers think that they're being left behind or feel that they're being left behind. And if we could focus on the middle class, if we can focus on workers when we talk about renewable energies and new economies, when we talk about American jobs plan or an infrastructure bill, if we're bringing American workers along and we have a by American provision, and we focus on the domestic steel and manufacturing. of what is going on in making sure that when we rebuild our roads, bridges, waterways, dams, water pipelines, infrastructure, our electricity grid that we bring workers along. If we do that, I believe that will chip away at the divide. So the PRO Act has a lot to do with giving unions the right to collectively bargain, to have fair elections, to put themselves in a position to regain ground that may have been taken away from unions' bargaining rights. over the last decade or so. You had mentioned Indiana and one of the first states to pass the right to work. So some might say, well, who might that impact? If you can go back in history, and I was there on the Indiana State Capitol stairs, there were over 15,000 men and women who showed up to protest the Right to Work Act, 15,000. The entire state capital was full of people on the outside and on the lawn and inside. And so we must remember that the middle class and working men and women and having the ability to have a fair wage is what's at stake. And so I'd be happy to have this discussion and dive into it, but that's a little bit of my perspective of where we come from. And as a member of Congress, how I view our labor unions in northwest Indiana.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: That's great. And I do want to say that I think There are many ways in addition to the right to work laws that were passed in the various states. There were lots of ways that at least our state administration was able to really chip away at unions. They made it more difficult to collect union dues. I think they just passed a law or considered a law that didn't required like first teacher unions require the school corporation to get them to get teachers to opt in every so often, which is was another hurdle to collect dues and other ways and you know many many businesses that used to be unions. Shops are not union shops anymore and it has of course driven down wages driven down benefits. And so that is why this is so important now. And I'd like to add a little bit, too, to the, you know, the number of unions that you mentioned. I always think that at this time that the service employees union is really important. These are the really low paid workers that really need a union more than a lot of industries. You know, so it's caregivers for the elderly, childcare workers, you know, mostly women, you know, in service industry jobs and wouldn't it be something? I know that we're talking about calling childcare infrastructure, but this would be another avenue for women in the workforce to, you know, get childcare so that they could get to work. And so I think that's a really important thing to remember too, that why this is so important, that this is a way for particularly women to overcome a lot of the hurdles that they have to fully participate in getting paid the same wages in whatever industry. So I know that the PRO Act, it's empowers the National Labor Relations Board a little more to enforce bad behavior by employers. And it does do away with the right to work laws, which is excellent, so that anyone who's working at a union shop and is benefiting from union services is required to pay into the union. I mean, that makes it fair in my mind. Another aspect of it is that, and we've seen a lot lately, this is another way that we've tipped away at unions is to call people contractors instead of employees. And so I think this pro act does something to address that, makes it harder for employers to call what we would consider employees independent contractors, which keeps them from getting any benefits as an employee. So, tell us what else is in this pro act and why this is going to help us.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: Well, you had mentioned the National Labor Relations Board and what that focuses on under the current law. It's unable to enforce its own orders. When an entity does not comply with the Board's orders, the National Labor Relations Board must seek enforcement through the U.S. Courts of Appeals. The bill would authorize the National Labor Relations Board to enforce its own orders requiring employers that failed to comply with the labor board to pay a civil monetary penalty up to $10,000 for each violation. And so what that does is it circumfence where people were going around the National Labor Relations Board in order to provide, instead of going to the courts, it has a direct violation. And so you had also mentioned the focus on the right to work and how that impacts. The right to work and ultimately I kind of want to go in a couple different areas, but I want to you know How the how we focused in Congress You know, we always have to keep in perspective COVID-19 and what we were under over the last year and a half. And there was a great deal of uncertainty in the workplace. A lot of the proactive had a lot to do with making sure OSHA was protecting workers because there were many essential workers were union labor that were out there on the roads and the bridges and the mills in the supermarkets in the classrooms. And so the PRO Act actually made sure that there was safe working conditions and that we were addressing COVID-19. And as a matter of priorities, we passed an apprenticeship program, early on in the legislative cycle in January, February, making sure that we put programming and resources towards apprenticeship programs so that we have a workforce that is developed and ready to go. throughout the United States and throughout North, Northwest Indiana, the first congressional district, putting our resources in there, making sure that it's accessible to women, making sure that it's accessible to minorities, making sure that it's accessible to those who want a job can prepare to be in the trades. I bring that up because the next thing we did is we passed the PROAC, making sure that we're protecting the middle class. And as we protect the middle class and we get them to work and they have the right to collectively bargain, they have the right to earn a fair wage, they have a right to safe working conditions, they have the right to a pension that is promised to them that they had put in for. So those things are extremely important because it was a matter of priority to make sure that we were doing that and immediately it was only a day apart we passed the rescue plan making sure that we were getting people a national strategic plan for people to get shots to be vaccinated making sure that dollars were spent on infrastructure and sent to the communities the school systems so that we could get kids back in school safely and making sure that we held up the economy. And so those are the things that were extremely important to us as a Congress and going forward now, now that we have the pro act and in passing the house, we have to make this law. We have to make sure that we have deliverables. So passing the United States Senate is extremely important, and having the Biden and Harris administration sign this into law is vital. And there has been no better friend to labor than the Biden and Harris administration. And what I want to see, make sure, as you mentioned, we passed it in the 107th Congress. Now we've passed it in the 117th, and the pro act is vital. And so we have to have your voices be heard if you're pro union and if you're a union member to the United States Senate. And so I kind of wanted to touch base on those things and be happy to answer any other questions you may have.
